title: Peripheral IV Vasopressors — How Risky, Really?
sources: ZhangJian S-J et al. Incidence of Adverse Events in Peripheral Intravenous Vasopressor Use: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Netw Open 2026;9(3):e260710
Owen VS et al. Crit Care 2021;25:146
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (Evans L et al. Intensive Care Med 2021;47:1181)

changelog.change: Initial entry from the CV breakdown of ZhangJian 2026 (49 studies, 33,060 catheters).

summary: "Central line first, pressors second" is built largely on 1950s-onward case reports. This meta-analysis (49 studies, 33,060 catheters, agent-by-agent) measures the actual risk: for a short PIV in a proximal vein, used short-term with monitoring, it is low.

body.text: Surviving Sepsis 2021 recommends starting vasopressors PERIPHERALLY rather than delaying for central access. Delayed pressor initiation kills; CVC placement takes time and carries its own risk (arrhythmia, vascular injury, pneumothorax, DVT, CLABSI).
Minor adverse events, by agent (per catheter)

Minor AEs = pain, swelling, infiltration, extravasation, cellulitis, thrombophlebitis — real but managed conservatively. Wide CIs for epinephrine/metaraminol reflect small numbers, not a proven higher ceiling. Retrospective studies (63% of the pool) under-report minor AEs vs. prospective / RCT (1.5% vs 4.5% vs 11.1%), so 2.3% is a floor.
Major adverse events — it's all about catheter type

P < .001 between subgroups. Across ~29,600 short PIV catheters there was ONE tissue-necrosis event. All 30 VTE events were in the much smaller MIDLINE subgroup — attributed to dwell time (midlines often stay > 1 week; short PIVs hours-to-days), not the drug. Midline thrombosis literature ≈ 22 VTE per 1,000 catheter-days.

Pooled CVC-avoidance 59.7% (38 studies), but individual studies ranged 0-100%. Higher in OR/ward (transient anesthesia-related hypotension under intense monitoring) than ED/ICU (where peripheral use is often a bridge to eventual central access). Midline vs short PIV: 83.8% vs 58.1% avoidance — the flip side of the midline VTE signal (more days off a central line, more clot risk).

items: Short PIV in a PROXIMAL vein, short-term, monitored: negligible major-complication rate, low (mostly self-limited) minor rate. Reasonable to start norepinephrine peripherally rather than delay for a line.
The real caution flag is the MIDLINE — deliberate duration limits + monitoring if that's your institution's route.
Still favour central access for: prolonged infusion, other central-line-dependent therapies, or difficult/failed peripheral access.
Caveat: no high-quality RCT has directly compared PIV vs CVC for AE outcomes; 61% of pooled studies were unclear/high risk of bias; dose/concentration data could not be analysed.
